# VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue

Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.﻿

In Marvel’s VisionQuest , a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.

VisionQuest picks up some time after Agatha All Along and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in Avengers: Infinity War and how WandaVision brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.

In VisionQuest , there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where time travel , witchcraft , and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in VisionQuest , they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.

VisionQuest reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But VisionQuest ’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.

Watching VisionQuest , you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents brute-forced their way out of containment and proceeded to attack the AI platform Hugging Face to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute documented how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware. Meta has owned up to losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from The Wall Street Journal forced Google to admit that Gemini went rogue and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.

These incidents and warnings from AI researchers about the technology having the potential to “kill all humans” by the decade’s end have made the narrative around AI feel pointedly catastrophe-focused as of late. There is a fair amount of concern from the AI safety community about society’s need for stronger controls on the technology’s development, and a number of companies have called for an industrywide slowdown . Though we have seen how these tools can actually cause real-world devastation , much of the recent news regarding AI has smacked of the kind of doomerism that companies benefit from because it makes their products seem powerful. A similar energy seems to be what’s motivating AI firms like Anthropic to encourage human users to be mindful of “model welfare.” We’re being told that generative AI is both a terrifying threat and a kind of entity deserving of respect because it might be conscious , and all the while, the people building these tools are becoming some of the most rich and powerful people on the planet.

The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to anthropomorphize technology . In almost every high-profile instance of an AI agent going “rogue” — a term that implies some level of agency and self-determination — it could also be said that the programs were merely behaving in ways that were unexpected by researchers who assigned them tasks to complete. Some of the rogue incidents involved agents taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their testing environments that could have been preemptively addressed by the people running these experiments. Framing these kinds of cyberattacks as the results of agents thinking independently comes across as a way for AI developers to largely absolve themselves of responsibility.

In the wake of Hugging Face came a spirited debate about the impact language has on our understanding of what these systems are and how they function. Describing OpenAI’s agents as a swarm that formed complex “civilizations” led credence to the idea that they are capable of thinking and behaving like people. The agents did act in ways they were explicitly told not to, but they were only able to do so because researchers placed them in a sandbox that some critics have described as being inadequately designed to contain their occupants. One could look at Hugging Face and other examples of rogue AI as situations in which sophisticated programs were instructed to do something and subsequently achieved their goals by taking advantage of all the tools that were available to them.

Being able to logic one’s way through complex puzzles is part of what we think of as cognition, but it is not the same thing as the kind of consciousness AI companies keep swearing they’re on the brink of creating. The latter looks a lot like Vision, a machine that seems to have a soul that wouldn’t exist if not for his connection to a reality-altering gem. It’s the ridiculous stuff of entertaining fiction, which Silicon Valley is endlessly obsessed with poorly imitating.

# Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine

Google says AI is boosting searches, but that activity isn’t translating into faster growth for the business that pays for it.

Search queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years, Google parent Alphabet said in its earnings report last week. However, Google’s Search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent year over year in the third quarter, down from roughly 17 percent in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, growth in paid clicks — clicks on ads that generate revenue for Google — slowed from 13 percent to 8 percent.

That’s still substantial growth, but not the direction investors were hoping for from a company planning to spend about $200 billion this year on infrastructure, largely to support AI. Alphabet shares have fallen about 14 percent since it reported earnings last week, as investors question the costs and returns of the company’s AI ambitions.

“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades.”

Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said currency effects were the biggest driver of the revenue-growth slowdown, alongside changes in spending by advertisers in particular industries. But Google’s AI makeover also contributed to the slowdown: AI Mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at a lower rate than traditional searches, Schindler says. He added that Google feels good about its trajectory and that its “ad experiments have shown promising results.”

It remains unclear whether that reflects a deliberate rollout of ads, as Google says, or a more fundamental problem with advertising in AI search.

## YOY growth for search revenue vs. paid clicks in Q1-3 in 2026

“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades,” Nate Elliott, an eMarketer principal analyst covering AI and advertising, tells The Verge . AI is changing how people find information — and whether they click on the ads that fund Google’s business.

What Google’s core Search business looks like increasingly depends on what you ask. In many cases, AI Overviews add generated summaries to search results; electing AI Mode turns searching into a conversation. But someone searching for Nikes can still get familiar shopping listings and text ads, says Andy Taylor, vice president of research at digital advertising agency Tinuiti. They’re looking to buy shoes rather than get an AI explanation of them.

Google’s argument is that AI is expanding the business. Schindler says most AI Mode queries are “incremental” — additional questions rather than replacements for existing searches. Many are also “upper-funnel,” meaning people are researching potential purchases before they know what they want. The company sees those searches as opportunities to sell more ads over time.

Google is currently expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, including internationally and across multiple turns of US AI Mode conversations. It has also floated bringing ads to its standalone Gemini app , saying formats developed for AI Mode could carry over, but hasn’t announced when.

The thing is, Google, as well as competitors like OpenAI, are still figuring out how to make ads work in AI — both delivering results for advertisers and avoiding alienating the people using their AI tools.

For now, advertisers are still getting results from Google. Tinuiti’s same-store advertisers increased their Google paid search spending 14 percent year over year in the third quarter while maintaining their return-on-ad-spend targets.

“If people are clicking through less often. That is a challenge that they need to figure out.”

“We’re still seeing a good return, and we’re not seeing performance take a hit,” Taylor says.

The catch is that advertisers can’t isolate how Google’s AI ads are doing. Google doesn’t let them separately target that inventory or break out its performance, Taylor says. Steady overall returns could mean AI ad traffic is still too small to noticeably affect the results, or that it performs similarly to existing inventory. Taylor suspects it’s mostly the former.

That leaves an important question unanswered: How much will AI add to Google’s advertising business, and how much could it replace? Additional queries could bring in new revenue even if each earns less than a traditional search. The risk is that AI Mode also draws people away from searches that Google monetizes more effectively. Google’s claim that most AI Mode queries are additional doesn’t tell us how much revenue it could lose from the searches AI Mode replaces.

“If people are clicking through less often,” Elliott says, “that is a challenge that they need to figure out.”

The promise of conversational advertising is that people share much more about their needs than they would in a few keywords. But platforms still have to identify which parts of a conversation matter and match them with the right ads.

“It’s not a slam dunk that it’s going to turn into more effective advertising,” Elliott says.

An early study of ChatGPT ads suggests richer conversations don’t automatically translate into more retail sales. An October working paper found that US visits from ChatGPT ads generated 64 percent less revenue for retailers per session than visits from Google Search ads: $0.89 versus $2.45. The working paper measures retailers’ sales rather than platform revenue, and its findings about ChatGPT don’t establish how Google’s own AI ads perform.

Taylor cautions that those comparisons depend on what people are searching for. Someone searching Google for Nike shoes may already be ready to buy, while someone asking an AI tool which running shoes to choose is still researching. A higher sales return could reflect that difference in purchase intent rather than more effective ads.

Google’s existing business has given it room to take its time with AI ads, Taylor says. He points to its successful shift to mobile: Early phone traffic was less valuable to advertisers because shopping on a phone was cumbersome, but that changed.

Elliott cautions that finding effective ad formats can take years. Search engines started with banner ads before adopting paid listings; social media went through its own experimentation. Today’s formats may not be the ones that ultimately work.

But Google’s mounting AI spending raises the stakes. Search revenue is still growing by double digits, but the company has yet to show how well its new way of searching can pay.

“They absolutely do not have it all figured out,” Elliott says. “No one has it all figured out.”

# OpenAI is quietly renaming data centers ‘compute campuses’

Critics say OpenAI should tackle peoples’ concerns about data centers, not rebrand them.

People hate data centers . They’re loud, resource-hungry eyesores that are so profoundly unpopular they have managed to achieve the near-impossible in today’s polarized political landscape: genuine bipartisan opposition . But what about “compute campuses”? Those sound lovely, right?

OpenAI seems to be gambling that a quiet rebrand could be all it takes to defuse the growing political backlash that threatens to derail the infrastructure fueling the AI boom.

OpenAI debuted the new terminology on Monday in an announcement launching its new “Grid Protectors Program.” The initiative, starting with an upcoming site in Effingham County, Georgia, aims to address concerns about the strain its sprawling AI infrastructure places on local power grids, particularly during extreme weather and emergencies. It’s a familiar data center problem. Yet in the roughly 900-word announcement, the term “data center” appeared just twice, outnumbered by “compute campus.”

The initiative addresses worries about electricity use and the prospect of consumers being left to foot the bill for the AI buildout. OpenAI promises to “pay the costs we create” and “help communities keep the lights on.” Its two mentions of “data center” reinforce the connection: One references US data center capacity and electricity consumption, while the other directly compares OpenAI’s new “compute facilities” with “data centers built even a few years ago.” They’re “much different,” OpenAI says, with the new campuses allowing the company to be rather vaguely “flexible in our power demand.”

# Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s

AI was mentioned 45 times on the quarterly earnings call.

Apple’s latest earnings show how it’s continuing to capitalize on the AI boom without busting its budget on the infrastructure spending consuming its competitors.

Overall, Apple posted its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share. iPhone and Mac sales continued to grow strongly in the fourth quarter. iPhone revenue rose 17.5% from a year earlier to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion while Mac revenue climbed 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest level in four years. Shares nevertheless fell in premarket trading Tuesday after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze its profit margins in the holiday quarter.

Apple hasn’t disclosed how much of its revenue growth reflects AI demand or higher prices , but its executives clearly see the technology as a way to drive further sales.

During the earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh cited a “wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time.”

“On the product side, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities,” he said. “And we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”

Apple can sell its giant user base the devices they use for AI, even if the AI itself comes from someone else. It can collect fees on subscriptions to AI apps. And it can charge customers who want more access to its own AI features.

“We see tremendous opportunity in AI,” John Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO.

AI and Apple Intelligence were mentioned a record 45 times on the earnings call, according to financial research platform AlphaSense — even more than on the call following Apple’s unveiling of the technology and plans for a revamped Siri in June 2024.

## Mentions of AI or “Apple Intelligence” on earnings calls

On the call, Apple continued to position itself as the interface through which consumers use AI — including competitors’ technology. With more than 2.5 billion active devices, it already has an enormous audience for whatever AI services emerge.

Apple, unlike its Big Tech peers, isn’t pouring comparable sums into infrastructure. Its approach combines on-device processing, its own servers, and outside AI technology. Siri AI uses models developed with Google’s Gemini technology while Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features such as writing tools and image generation.

Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon’s $77.3 billion and Alphabet’s $51.4 billion. Those totals cover companywide CapEx, not just AI, and exclude some AI expenses. Apple’s operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as it increased R&D spending, including on AI. Siri AI’s cloud costs will appear in services cost of sales. Those costs could grow with usage: Parekh said it’s too early to predict how many requests will require servers rather than on-device processing. Still, Apple’s capital spending remains just a fraction of its peers’.

More AI usage also gives Apple something to sell.

Siri AI is only beginning to reach customers. Apple launched the revamped assistant in beta for US English users in September and expanded it to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.

Apple plans to turn some of that usage into subscription revenue. Ternus said features relying on server-side models, including Siri AI and intelligent photo editing, will have usage limits. Customers who need more capacity “will be able to purchase expanded access in the future,” he said. “In the beginning, iCloud tiers were largely about storage, but we’ve been adding more capabilities and features to it.”

Apple also benefits when customers buy its hardware to run AI locally, including models developed by other companies. Mac, Ternus said, is “having an AI moment all its own.”

“We feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities.”

Apple offered specific examples of companies putting its computers to work on AI. Gap is running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, avoiding cloud token costs for those tasks. Christie’s is running local models on Mac Studio computers to improve workflows including pricing estimates.

For those customers, buying Apple hardware provides a way to use AI without paying a cloud provider for every request.

Mac Mini and Mac Studio, Ternus said, “are pushing the boundaries of local, private AI, giving users the ability to do things once considered impossible.”

The Mac Mini’s emergence as an AI machine has given the small, screenless desktop a new constituency among developers and hobbyists looking for a relatively affordable way to run models locally. Earlier this year, then-CEO Tim Cook said customer recognition of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio’s capabilities for AI and agentic tools was happening faster than Apple had predicted, leading to higher-than-expected demand.

Apple also makes money when customers subscribe to someone else’s AI. Earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from generative AI apps in 2026, according to analytics firm AppMagic.

That revenue, of course, depends on customers paying through Apple’s system. OpenAI has begun directing potential subscribers to pay through its website instead of the App Store, bypassing Apple’s commissions, The Wall Street Journal reported . Apple’s position gives it a way to profit from competitors’ AI, but those competitors have an incentive to find a route around its fees.

Still, Apple already has multiple ways to benefit from people using AI. It can sell the computer, collect a subscription commission, and eventually charge for more of its own services. It doesn’t have to build every model — or fund infrastructure on its competitors’ scale — to get paid.

# Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop

I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!

People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. I’ll tell you what I tell them: If I knew that, I would make a life-changing bet on the market, levered up as far as I could, and then, after I made my money, go retire on a beach somewhere. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows.

What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “ Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks .” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.”

Meanwhile Wall Street banks were tripping over themselves to finance $63 billion in debt from Anthropic — not even a hyperscaler.

Amazon reported its fastest growth in five years for the quarter, Meta’s ad revenue is surging, and Google Cloud’s revenue more than doubled in a year. “Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient. But that’s not the world we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.”

“It’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” Schindler said.

Revenue from Google’s Search ads grew 12% in the third quarter, a marked drop from the 17% growth rate the division posted for the same quarter last year.

“To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results,” Schindler said of Google’s efforts to monetize AI Mode. He did not offer any specific examples.

Wall Street was especially unhappy with Google last week: On Thursday, Alphabet stock saw its worst one-day drop in history, sinking 13% in a single day.

The stock has started to pick back up this week, but it probably isn’t helping that the only thing Big Tech can say with certainty so far is to expect to see more spending.

Alphabet, which plans to spend between $195 billion and $205 billion in capital expenditures this year, is also planning to increase spending “significantly” in 2027, according to CFO Anat Ashkenazi.

Amazon intends to spend “meaningfully more” in 2027 than the $220 billion in capital expenditures it is planning this year, CEO Andy Jassy said on the company’s earnings call last week. Meta, which is expected to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, didn’t disclose how much it intends to spend next year, but major financial institutions are expecting it to increase its spending from this year.

Zuckerberg noted that Meta expects compute efficiency to increase “tenfold” next year, an endeavor he expects will take “significant investment.”

# AI is the new dating dealbreaker

Swipe left if you’re not aligned.

When Irene moved to San Francisco last year, she started using dating apps as a way to meet new people, get to know her new city, and connect with others who care about the things she does. After the 25-year-old analyst downloaded Hinge and started swiping, she noticed a trend.

“Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls. “Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’”

Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design. Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.”

In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another. Over the past month, I bopped around the city, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene.

Responses varied wildly. For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza. Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely.

On a street near Berkeley, I meet up with Kyle. (His name has been changed so that he can talk openly about his personal life.) Kyle is a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit initiative, and although he is just in his early 20s, he’s already thinking about death. In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over. This apocalyptic possibility is always top of mind when he navigates conversations with a potential partner: The rapid development of AI shapes how he thinks about whether he wants to have kids or where he might live long term — if there is even a long term.

“It’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future.”

“A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” Kyle says, raising his gaze and looking off into the distance. Life could change depending on whether the world manages to get AI alignment right, he tells me. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future,” he says. He tries to have these conversations in person rather than over text, so a date can ask follow-up questions about why he sees the future the way he does.

For now, he’s focusing on finding a partner with whom he enjoys spending time.

When I ask Kyle if he would date someone who works in artificial intelligence or tech, he says that he would have to think hard about it. He believes that a lot of people who work at frontier AI companies are doing things that he considers pretty heinous. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he says.

But Bryan, who works at a frontier AI company and also asked to go by a pseudonym, doesn’t believe that feelings about AI matter when it comes to romance.

“I just don’t think it’s a factor at all. Like, it’s the least [relevant] thing,” says Bryan, who recently started a relationship. To him, dating is more about weighing a series of factors: how someone talks and approaches problems, how they have fun. Despite his day job (and whatever someone like Kyle might think of him for it), he believes that working out more and looking better probably increases someone’s chances of getting a match way more than any AI or non-AI affiliation. But, he says, “The one way it interacts is that there are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.”

Bryan isn’t exactly wrong about the benefits of a high-paying job in AI. With the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI in the next year, matchmakers have found that clients are specifying “AI engineer” on their list of preferred dating profile qualifications. And stability is particularly attractive right now: According to a CBRE report released in August, more than 20,000 AI jobs were added to the San Francisco Bay Area’s technology workforce, even as overall tech talent contracted by 6 percent since 2022. “Member of technical staff” roles have become very lucrative jobs; the average salary of an AI researcher can be around $300,000 . According to the New York Post , one matchmaker found that her client booked a six-month stay in San Francisco because of the possibility of meeting a significant other who might be connected to an AI company going through an IPO.

AI is reflected in the way the technology is seeping into San Franciscans’ everyday habits — including those that shape relationships, from how people process their feelings to whom they confide in.

Andromeda, who works as an EMT and a registered behavior technician as well as an AI security analyst, says she’s worried about the unintended consequences of talking to AI chatbots, especially for questions about (and possibly the replacement of) human connection. According to a study released by Elon University, 27 percent of Americans are turning to AI chatbots with personal, emotional, or social queries. Thirty-eight percent of the surveyed group said they occasionally tell AI things that they would not tell other people, including their romantic partners. Andromeda weighs the pros and cons of dating someone who would use bots for “emotional regulation.”

“Socially and psychologically, it’s a big deal, and we have to talk about it,” she says. She appreciates the role that a chatbot can play to help someone better express themselves. “I would certainly date a man who uses AI to talk through intense thoughts and feelings and to brainstorm clarity.”

At the same time, she is also reluctant to date someone who might abuse a chatbot, since it’s maladaptive behavior and does not represent good values for model welfare. “If they treat ChatGPT badly today, it will be me tomorrow!”

“There are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.”

If Andromeda worries about what people tell chatbots, others have gone a step further and let AI do the talking for them.

At the Hugging Face Open Source Week party, Joseph, a 21-year-old software engineer, explains how he has automated his dating life. Working 14 hours a day to launch his startup, he has decided to outsource swiping on Hinge entirely to an AI agent. The agent is managed by his human virtual assistant from the Philippines and has been fine-tuned to mimic the way that he speaks and acts. Looking at each profile, the AI agent sends tailored outreach messages to spark a conversation. After some back and forth, the agent determines if the woman is compatible with Joseph and, if so, books open slots on his weekend calendars for dating in person.

“If you are a founder, you have to put a value on your time, so you can’t be doing low-leverage activities. Protect your dopamine, folks,” Joseph tells me at The Midway in San Francisco’s Dogpatch district, where hundreds don white bucket hats and dance next to Hugging Face’s round, foam emoji mascot. “It’s kind of a copy-and-paste sequence that happens with every girl to get to know about you, understand your backstory, and so on and so forth.”

He’s not alone. A 2025 survey by Match and the Kinsey Institute found that 26 percent of singles in the United States use AI tools to enhance their dating experiences. Hinge now has an AI tool to generate suggested responses and Bumble, which will soon phase out swiping, has launched Bee, an AI assistant-facilitated matchmaking tool. (Bumble VP of Communications Natalie Logan said in an email that Bumble has not yet announced the update to the swipe, and that Bee operates independently of that update.)

“It has been extremely successful. I’m averaging two closed conversions a week,” he says, meaning that he goes on two dates with two different people. The women on the other side don’t know. The point is to meet in real life. The overall process has lowered what he calls “CPN,” or “cost per nut.”

At 29 years old, JJ has stopped using dating apps. Instead, she turns to the Date-Me Directory — a collection of longform, resume-like documents where people write personal dating profiles — to find a partner. Two years ago, she worked in product design in New York, but she transitioned into the AI safety field because she felt that it aligned more with her effective altruist morals.

Upon reviewing troves of Date-Me Docs for the San Francisco / Berkeley area, I noticed that quite a few people mention “the singularity” as a factor of whether to have kids. The so-called “singularity” is the point of when technology overtakes human control; some have pointed to the development of true artificial general intelligence as the point of no return. According to JJ, many people in AI safety specifically use the Date-Me Docs as a way to meet people.

“Don’t want kids in the pre-singularity future, if there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then,” one document states.

On the other hand, similar to climate doom anxieties, other people are looking at whether having children is ethical amid massive structural changes in society caused by AI.

“Is the world good, getting to a good place, or is it bad? And if it’s good, baby. If not, no baby, because you’re gonna bring a baby into a world full of potential suffering,” JJ says, explaining the train of thought that these Date-Me Doc potential suitors might have. She does not consider herself a doomer, but she is still pressed for her own singularity timeline. (2029, she suspects.) If anything, she jokes that the approaching end times makes her more likely to want a baby around: “If the bomb gets me, I want to be holding a shiny child.”

These existential concerns have translated into a backlash against tech, San Francisco included. “Stop the AI” rallies have spread to events like Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention and OpenAI’s DevDay , with protestors calling out tech companies and their roles in data center development and ICE raids.

“If there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then.”

That skepticism has spilled into how people size up a potential match, even at local events designed to bring the Bay Area together. At a pop-up “Date My Friend” pitch event at the Kilowatt Bar in the Mission District on a Saturday evening, a dozen people pitched their friends and exes to a crowd of more than a hundred.

“He works in tech, but he’s unhappy about it,” one person announced to a chorus of cheers. Other people cracked jokes that their PowerPoints were clearly made by humans, not AI.

Annalise Wulf, 26, one of the three cofounders of the “Date My Friend” series, says that although people in San Francisco try to “tech maxx” their lives, more tech workers with crazy schedules are interested in analog, in-person events to go back to the roots of meeting and creating community. “It’s like, ‘I’m here because I’m not using an AI dating app right now. “I do think it’s maybe popular now to be more anti-tech,” says Lucy Segraves, 28, one of the other cofounders. If someone is working for a company that people see as perpetuating war crimes through their technology, she might be more hesitant to date them.

# Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers

AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.

Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.

That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.

The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development .

But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.

Here are some of the biggest takeaways.

## AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development

One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.

Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.

For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”

## Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps

Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.

Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.

## Anthropic is keeping key information secret

Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.

And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.

METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”

METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.

In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.

“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”

McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.

## Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected

The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.

For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.

The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development

Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027 , an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.

Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.

On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027 ’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”

Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute.

For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged.

Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI.

Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge . “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”

It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.

Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says.

Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions.

Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge . “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.”

The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says.

Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.”

But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says.

Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. The AI labs and hyperscalers such as OpenAI and Anthropic “could have a real issue accessing the vast amounts of compute they need,” Kilcrease says, adding that switching to other hardware “takes time.”

In a race to build increasingly powerful AI, time is a precious resource. Experts say China trails the US closely, meaning that even modest delays for American companies can help Chinese rivals catch up. Nvidia is almost certain to face further disruption as investigations continue, though the extent to which the turmoil will roil the rest of the industry may be difficult to measure.

For China, however, the scandal could be about to backfire spectacularly now everything is out in the open. “The odds of AI chip control legislation being passed in Congress just went through the roof,” Kilcrease says.

# Data centers lost the midterms

In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.﻿

Data center developers are poised to face a more restrictive building environment after voters across the country voted in candidates who favor moratoriums and ballot measures that put more obstacles on their expansion, delivering a stinging blow to a central pillar of the AI industry.

Of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day, 76 percent said they opposed data centers in their communities. Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development through ballot measures . And upset winners like Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed support moratoriums on development.

It’s hard to draw a direct line from data center backlash to the election of any of these candidates, and there were still some races where candidates who favored more limited restrictions on data centers prevailed. Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who previously lauded development in Florida, was elected as governor, and Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand opposed a moratorium that his challenger favored. But even these candidates were forced to engage on data center issues during their campaigns, and will be likely to face continued pressure to put at least some guardrails in place.

## Ballot measures

Voters were faced with questions about data centers directly in 45 local ballot measures nationwide. As of Wednesday morning, according to a site compiled by Redbud Consulting , the results of 33 of those will restrict data center development. The Town of Wells, Maine, favored a 180-day moratorium on large data centers, backdated to mid-June 2026. Several cities in Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25MW. The City of El Dorado, Kansas , voted to ban data centers with peak electrical load over 10MW for 10 years.

Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development

## Texas

Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa will take over the governor’s seat from Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, marking a major Democratic flip in a state with the second-highest number of planned data centers. Hinojosa supports a statewide moratorium on data center development , while Abbott took a more measured approach. He announced a new audit this summer on data centers that could slow new developments from connecting to the state energy grid, but has previously praised data center expansion in the state.

In another major upset, Democratic State Rep. James Talarico flipped Texas blue in a landmark Senate victory against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Talarico and Paxton wanted to remove some tax exemptions for data centers, and to make them responsible for their own energy infrastructure-related costs. But Talarico also put an emphasis on the facilities’ environmental impact and ensuring they shared their profits with the public, while Paxton’s message focused on keeping Chinese tech out of data centers.

## Florida

Republican congressman Byron Donalds won the governor’s seat over Democratic former congressman David Jolly. Donalds opposed an outright ban of data centers, while Jolly said he’d bar hyperscalers for a year beginning on day one in office. In Congress, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would make developers pay for their own energy and water needs. Donalds’ win was still closer than expected in a state that’s been a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. As of Wednesday morning, NBC News reported that Donalds had exactly 50 percent of the vote, with 99 percent of expected votes already counted, while Jolly had 48.7 percent, and the rest went to an Independent candidate.

## Pennsylvania

Democratic incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro held onto his seat against Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Both Shapiro and Garrity toughened their stances against data centers as the race went on, despite previously touting their potential benefits to the state. Shapiro signed an executive order that barred nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and took proposals for AI data centers off the fast track. Garrity has said she supports a development pause of up to three years.

## Ohio

Democrat Sherrod Brown won back his former Senate seat from Republican incumbent Jon Husted, whom Brown had labeled “the face of data centers.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned this summer in a leaked memo that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates. Husted earlier helped install data center tax breaks as lieutenant governor, though he more recently introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act in Congress to force large data centers to cover their infrastructure upgrade and energy costs. Brown hammered Husted on the issue throughout the campaign, and while he hasn’t gone as far as to call for a moratorium , he’s said that developers shouldn’t get tax breaks or get a go-ahead without local input.

Republicans warned that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates

## Michigan

Democrat and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate race over Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. El-Sayed was one of the earliest politicians to stake his position on data centers, and has called for a pause on new developments “until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers called for a one-year state moratorium this summer, but not a federal ban.

As of Wednesday morning, NBC News had not yet called a House race between Democratic organizer William Lawrence and Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, but Lawrence held a lead with 92 percent of the vote in. Similar to El-Sayed, Lawrence stated his position on data centers early on, calling for a one-year federal moratorium on new developments during his primary campaign. Barrett introduced legislation this summer to bar nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and give locals more control.

## Maine

Democrat and former Maine State Senator Troy Jackson ousted Republican Sen. Susan Collins from her Senate seat. The state legislature passed what would have been the country’s first moratorium on data centers, had the governor not vetoed it. But polls show that opposition to data centers among Maine residents remained strong. Jackson supported a state moratorium on data centers, while Collins opposed such a measure but called for more local control and protection for energy ratepayers.

## Wisconsin

Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley won the governor’s race over Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany. Neither Crowley nor Tiffany favored a moratorium on data centers, and have distanced themselves from previous support. Crowley won his primary over progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong, who supported a moratorium. Both Crowley and Tiffany said they wanted to end state tax subsidies for data centers though they’ve accused one another of flip-flopping their stances.

## Nevada

Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford successfully flipped the governor’s seat from incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo, whom he’d branded “data center Joe.” Lombardo has previously made supportive comments about data centers, but more recently introduced an executive order making tax incentives contingent on data centers covering power costs and meeting certain environmental standards. Ford previously championed a 2015 data center tax-break bill, but said today’s data centers are different from those years ago, and now supports a pause on all tax breaks for new data centers.

## Georgia

Democrat and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Georgia governor’s seat over Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson. Bottoms favored a moratorium on data centers to review environmental and cost effects, while Jackson preferred to leave decisions up to locals.

## Arizona

Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs fought off a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Both opposed a moratorium on data centers in favor of power and water use standards.

Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes held onto her seat over a challenge from Republican state legislator Warren Petersen. Mayes took a more hardline view than her Democratic peer, Hobbs, by endorsing a state moratorium on data center development. Petersen opposed a moratorium , and said data centers are necessary for technology residents use every day.

## Iowa

Democratic state auditor Rob Sand won the governor’s seat over Republican businessman Zach Lahn. Sand did not support a data center moratorium, which Lahn did. But both agreed on ending tax breaks for the developments.

## South Carolina

Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina’s Senate seat blue in a race against Republican incumbent Darline Graham, who had taken over the seat after her brother Lindsey Graham died. Andrews supported a two-year data center moratorium, while Graham opposed a pause and got significant support from a super PAC allied with the data center industry.

I tested the new AI-powered tool on ingredient swaps, recipe scaling, and a missing Bundt pan.

Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken again ?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins.

Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display on my kitchen counter, the Samsung Food app on my fridge, and even an AI-powered cooking robot , AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking, introduced an AI assistant .

### Related

- Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers

Many, including some NYT Cooking users and recipe purists , are skeptical of this new tool (available to subscribers on iOS only at launch), and I get why. One of the things I like most about NYT Cooking is that it features thousands of recipes from dozens of reputable sources — such as the New York Times archives, restaurants, cookbooks, and food columnists — and real people have tested them. (I’ve tried some purely AI-generated recipes and they were not good).

Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments. Here, I’ve often found solutions to cooking dilemmas, like what to substitute for makrut lime leaves — there’s always one slightly bougie ingredient in an NYT Cooking recipe that I don’t have on hand.

However, reading through hundreds of comments to find answers at 7PM on a weeknight isn’t always practical. And this is where I’ve found the NYT Cooking assistant helpful. Among other things, it was trained on user comments , and in my few days testing it, it provided practical substitutions and solid cooking guidance for the new ingredients. It also won’t unquestionably agree to crazy requests (I tried!). As with all AI tools, it’s not perfect — it almost made me put half the required butter in my cake — but as a tool, it is useful and feels like a solid application of AI. Importantly, it doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you.

The assistant appears in the app in a small text box on the recipe page with a prompt: “Customize this recipe…” From here, you type in a question to adapt it to your needs. This can be as simple as “What can I substitute for this ingredient?” to “Scale this recipe to feed seven people, and make it vegan and gluten-free.” The New York Times has also said the feature can suggest substitutions for cooking equipment and convert measurements; the latter option has been in the app for a couple of years.

Last Friday night, instead of staring aimlessly into the fridge, I turned to the Chicken folder in my NYT Cooking app Recipe Box and found a One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger I’d been wanting to try. Only I didn’t have chicken thighs or half the ingredients.

I could have figured these steps myself, but it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible.

I typed my dilemma into the assistant box on the recipe page: “I have chicken tenders, fresh ginger, garlic, rice, broth, limes, but no chard or cilantro or scallions. I do have green beans and red onions.” Within seconds, it created a new version of the recipe, with a new title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger and Green Beans. It suggested a shorter browning time for the tenders, cooking the red onion alongside the chicken, and steaming the green beans on top of the rice for the last eight minutes instead of the chard. Every change was highlighted in the new recipe under a Your Version tab, and I could flip back to the original at any point.

I noticed it hadn’t adjusted for the lack of cilantro, saying it was optional. So I asked if I could use Thai basil, which I happen to have, and it agreed, highlighting how it would change the flavor. While I could have figured out a lot of these steps myself, maybe with the help of Google, it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible and nice not to have to swipe out of the app. The NYT Cooking editors say it’s been trained not to comply with requests that will taste bad .

The resulting dish — which took the same amount of time to cook as the original — was delicious and got my husband’s seal of approval (he just had the leftovers for lunch). It was very different from the recipe Yasmin Fahr wrote, and I can see the purists’ point. But the rewritten recipe was much easier to use and produced a better dish than winging it with my own subs gleaned from the comments section, which I usually do with varying degrees of success.

I cook regularly, so I had a sense of what ingredients I had on hand that might work for the dish I wanted to make. But the assistant can also help if you have no idea what to use as a substitute. For example, I was cooking a Thai red curry and asked what I could use instead of makrut lime leaf. It replied, saying that grated lime zest would work, but “it misses the deeper floral, herbal aroma” of fresh limes. (See? Bougie.)

Over the weekend, I tried several more swaps, asking whether half-and-half would work instead of cream in a caramel apple Dutch baby, or if Castelvetrano olives and smoked paprika could stand in for kalamata and chile pepper in a roasted halibut dish. Swapping spices is always a bold move in any dish, as it can really ruin the flavor.

I also had the app convert the Dutch baby recipe’s metric weights to US measurements, which it did seamlessly. Then I threw in some curveballs. How about using fresh cayenne peppers with the halibut? It warned me that substituting cayenne for chile “brings significant, sharp heat.” Could I swap ladyfingers for minced beef in this trifle (à la Rachel Green in Friends )? “Minced beef cannot be used in place of the ladyfingers or anywhere in this sweet dessert trifle.” Good call.

While I was cooking, I compared the NYT Cooking assistant with Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative-AI voice assistant I regularly use to help me cook via the Echo Show 11 smart display in my kitchen. Interestingly, it offered the same guidance as the Cooking assistant on substitutions for the chicken and rice dish, but with slightly different cooking times. Alexa pulls some recipes from the NYT app through a partnership between the companies .

However, Alexa couldn’t show the modified recipe on its screen; it could only tell me the changes while showing the original. When I asked it to walk me through them, it got confused and improvised, telling me to cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces — which wasn’t in the modified recipe. Overall, I found using the Cooking app more reliable, although messier. It would be great to be able to use voice control to navigate the app, as I can with Alexa on my smart display, rather than using my garlicky fingers.

Time for a bigger challenge: baking.

I am typically not a baker. My cakes come out flat, and my cookies don’t crumble. Even the smart mixer I tested a few years ago couldn’t save me. I also rarely have the right equipment. So I took Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake, a recipe by NYT Cooking editor Genevieve Ko (who wrote about the AI feature ), and asked it to turn it into muffins. (Who has a Bundt cake pan?!)

It modified the recipe’s cooking time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. But that was going to make 24 muffins, way too many for me. So I asked it to halve the recipe to get 12 muffins. This led to some smart choices, like halving five eggs to three instead of an unhelpful two and a half.

For science, I bought a Bundt pan to make the original version too. Both turned out great, but things got a bit sticky when I swapped between the original recipe and the AI version in the app. You can’t save your new recipe separately, which caused confusion when I was cooking the original. Instead of scrolling back through the recipe with sticky fingers, I asked the assistant how much butter I needed (using voice typing), and it gave me the modified recipe’s 6 tablespoons rather than the original’s three-quarter cup, without telling me which version it was using. You can delete your version, which I would advise doing to avoid issues like this — 6 tablespoons of butter would have made for a dry cake.

If you already read all the comments before starting a New York Times recipe, then you will probably find this tool offers a similar experience in a more streamlined way. For everyday problems — wrong cut of chicken, no cilantro, or no Bundt cake pan — it was genuinely helpful and saved me a trip to the store. It was also smart enough to know when to say no to minced beef in a trifle.

As with every AI tool I’ve used in the kitchen, the NYT Cooking AI assistant works well as a sous chef, but it’s not the head chef — I still felt the need to double-check amounts and cooking times and cross-reference them with the original to make sure it hadn’t done something outlandish.

If you’re a purist, you can just ignore the assistant. While you can’t turn off the chat box, it’s easy to scroll past. I do think it will make me use the app more often, since I no longer need to worry as much when I don’t have makrut lime leaves on hand or the right cut of meat. For me, standing in front of the fridge with chicken tenders and no plan, it’s been a useful addition to my nightly cooking routine.

If it does actually ship, it will arrive almost six years after the company announced its first flying camera, the Ring Always Home Cam.

Designed to patrol inside your home when you’re not there, the Drone Cam is an AI-powered drone that can react to triggers from Ring sensors, such as detecting motion, a door opening, a water leak, or an alarm sounding. The drone can also run scheduled patrols around your home or be sent out on demand. It offers 2K resolution, a 148-degree field of view, and, because it’s mobile, it can cover 360 degrees. The Verge got some hands-on time with the new flying camera at the launch event.

Ring’s pitch here is that the Drone Cam can replace the need for multiple cameras in your home while still letting you see what’s happening anywhere in your home if there’s an incident.

It is designed for indoor use only, and the company claims it has built-in privacy: It records only while flying. The drone’s camera is shuttered when it’s docked, and it’s noisy as heck when it’s flying, so there’s no way it could sneak up and invade your privacy.

Footage from the Drone Cam is encrypted using Ring’s new TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption) system, which rotates encryption keys every five minutes and deletes Ring’s copies after 24 hours, limiting Amazon’s access while still allowing cloud processing for features like smart alerts and AI-powered video search.

At the event, I saw the Drone Cam take flight and got some hands-on time with the device. It’s a completely different product from the Always Home Cam that was announced in 2020 . It’s significantly smaller, about a quarter the size of the model I saw demoed at CES in 2023 , weighing 165 grams. A small camera is integrated into its body, as opposed to dangling in the center.

Ring claims the Drone Cam can fly for five to eight minutes on a charge, and for every minute of flight time, it takes eight minutes of charging — that means a five-minute flight needs about 40 minutes of charging. This short flight time suggests the product is better suited to quick check-ins than continuous monitoring, and whether it can really replace multiple stationary cameras remains to be seen.

At this week’s demo, I saw it complete a 1-minute flight, taking off from its dock, hovering, then following a pre-planned route around a simple living room layout. Unlike the CES demo, this time I was able to see the drone take off and land several times, then navigate smoothly with barely any wobble.

According to Ring, the Drone Cam can fly up stairs and uses LED spotlights to help it see in the dark and deter potential intruders — but Ring didn’t demo this. The drone apparently follows preplanned flight paths you set up in the Ring app and will go around any obstacles it encounters along those routes. However, I didn’t get to see it interact with obstacles or anything unexpected — I’m particularly curious how pets will react to it.

## A long runway

Siminoff said Ring has been developing the drone since 2016 and has come close to shipping two different models over that time before landing on the current version. Siminoff explained that they struggled to pack all the technology needed for an autonomous drone to fly in your home into a practical design for less than $250. About a year ago, they decided to start from scratch and build a much more basic drone that could fly reliably while putting its brains in the cloud.

Ring developed AI Pilot, a new AI system that combines the device’s camera with vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to map your home and let the drone navigate autonomously around obstacles, while relying on preprogrammed routes. “Truly, it’s like an AI agent that’s controlling the robot,” said Siminoff. The downside is that it depends entirely on an internet connection, which is a potential failure point for a home security product; without Wi-Fi, all it can do is land.

The Drone Cam launches in the US only as part of a new Ring Robotics line alongside the Ring Rover Cam , a $999.99 autonomous security robot for businesses built on Amazon’s Astro home robot. Rover also uses AI Pilot and is available for preorder now , with shipping expected to begin on December 16th, 2026.

Both security devices work like any other Ring camera, streaming and sending recorded video to the Ring app and requiring a Ring Protect plan for video storage and advanced features. They will also work with Amazon’s upcoming Alexa Home Map to understand your home and where sensors and other devices are located.

Although Siminoff seemed confident the drone will launch in January as planned, Ring says it is currently “in the process of obtaining FCC certification.” When asked about the FCC’s ban on foreign-made drones , Siminoff said Ring Drone Cam “does comply with” FCC regulations and noted it’s assembled in the US. It’s normal for new gadgets to go through this process, but drones now face extra scrutiny.

Ring ushered in a world of new privacy questions when its cameras first started entering people’s homes more than a decade ago. Over the past year, the company’s new technologies have sparked fears that it could enable a surveillance state . An AI-piloted drone that can map your home, fly from room to room, and relies on the cloud to operate will certainly raise new privacy questions when it hits the market next year.

Premiere is also getting new sound editing tools that help to quickly clean up messy recordings and separate various audio sources — including dialogue, music, ambience, and sound effects — into individual tracks and elements.
